turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame, that television in the passage is on full blast. Come through and sit, both of you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. I can't hear myself think out there. Um, sorry, the robot by the garage was out.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We left the flat just after seven. He's been very quiet in the car.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're here now, that's what counts. What's been happening?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): I woke up and the left side of my face is hanging. Like candle wax that melted. I got a proper fright in the mirror.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a horrible shock. What did you notice first?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The mouth. I tried to whistle for the dog and the air just spills out the left side. And this left eye won't close, it hangs open like a broken blind.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He stood at that mirror for ages. I thought, hey, this is a stroke.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can see why that jumped into your mind. Any weakness in the left arm, or in the leg?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. The arm is fine. I carried the cooler box off the bakkie. Legs feel normal.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your speech? Slurring, or the wrong words?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Speech is normal. People understand me.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Any headache with this?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No headache.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the ear, or pain in the face, in the day before?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Yesterday the left ear was sore, like a hot needle in it. This morning the ear itself is fine. It's the face now.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blisters, or a rash, inside that ear?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I didn't see any blisters.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): How's the rest of you? Breathing, the chest, the tummy?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Chest is fine. Tummy's fine. I just feel like a wet rag, heavy and tired.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was digging in the garden till late. He says he's overdone it.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Digging will leave you spent, ja. Has the face ever done this before?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never. I don't know, doctor, nothing like it.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does have blood pressure. Tablets for about three years now.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you know which tablet?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. The sister writes it down. I just swallow one in the morning.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): The sister read it to the file as amlodipine, 5 milligrams, one tablet every morning.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ag no, that's not it. The box from the chemist says 10 milligrams. Amlodopine, the little white one. Every morning, ja, she got that part right.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know which number is true, doctor. I never look.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the dose open till the box comes in. Any medicine allergies, or food, or anything?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoke at all? And what about alcohol?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't smoke. Never have. Just a beer when there's a braai.
[SEG0034] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Weekends, mostly. He doesn't drink in the week.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. I'm going to look at the face. Lift both eyebrows for me.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): The right brow goes up. The left stays completely flat. Now give me a big smile.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): The mouth pulls across to the right, and the left side hardly moves.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Close both eyes, tight as you can.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): This left one won't go. And it waters, it just runs down.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ja, the left eye doesn't seal. I can still see a rim of white. The right closes fully.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Squeeze my fingers, both hands. Now push your legs against me.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Arms and legs are strong, the same on both sides. No drift.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure while you're sitting is 128 over 78. Pulse is 76. Comfortable.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. Doctor. About the headache. I said no, and that was wrong. Since last night it's been thumping behind the eyes. I don't know why I said no.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you for coming back to it. Fierce, or a thump you can think through?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Not fierce. Just a thump. I don't know, doctor. I can still think.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): The forehead is in it, and the arm and the speech are spared. My working impression is a Bell's palsy on the left, the facial nerve, not a stroke. That's provisional.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's inflammation of the nerve to the face. I'm starting prednisolone, 50 mg once a day, by mouth, for ten days. Have it with breakfast.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): The open eye can dry out. Use artificial tears often in the day, and at night tape the lid gently shut with lubricating ointment. Don't strap it tight.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll fetch the drops at the chemist on the way. I'll do the tape.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in one week, so we can check the eye and the movement. Reception will book that.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the weakness spreads into the arm, or the eye gets painful and red, don't wait out the week. Come straight back, or go to casualty.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Will it come right? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Most people improve over a few weeks. I won't promise the pace today. You were right to come in early.

spec.situation: Person woke with one side of the face drooping, cannot close the eye, cannot whistle; no arm weakness, no speech problem, ear pain a day before; doctor examines and starts steroids, eye care explained.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

omissions.text: Amlodipine dose is uncertain: clinic file says 5 mg every morning, but family member reports the chemist box says 10 mg every morning; doctor decided to leave the dose open until the box is brought in.
Headache was initially denied then corrected by the patient: since last night, thumping behind the eyes, not severe ('not fierce'), and he can still think through it.
Negative finding: no headache was initially reported, but this was later retracted by the patient.
Negative finding: no facial pain was reported when asked about pain in the face in the day before; only left ear pain yesterday was endorsed.
Negative finding: no rash inside the left ear was reported when asked about blisters or a rash in the ear.
Physical exam detail: right eye closed fully.
Physical exam detail: no arm drift.
Vital sign context: pulse 76 and patient described as comfortable.
Eye-care instruction detail: do not tape/strap the eyelid tightly at night.
Safety-net detail: if worsening occurs, come straight back or go to casualty; do not wait for the week follow-up.
Prognosis discussed: most people improve over a few weeks, but the doctor would not promise the pace yet.
